title: "Menstrual Health Legislation and K-12 Chronic Absenteeism"
subtitle: "Exploring the Association Between State Menstrual Health and Hygiene Policy and Female Student Absenteeism in US Public Schools"
abstract: "This study examines whether statewide menstrual health and hygiene (MHH) legislation is associated with reduced chronic absenteeism among female students in US public schools. Using three years of federal EDFacts data (academic years 2020–2021 through 2022–2023) covering traditional public school districts across all 50 states, we compared what share of each district's chronically absent students were female, contrasting states with enacted MHH legislation against states without it. Across 11 of 12 demographic subgroups and all three school years, chronically absent students in enacted-policy states were significantly less likely to be female than in no-policy states — a small but statistically significant and highly consistent gap. This gap was largest among economically disadvantaged students, the group most likely to face menstrual product access barriers due to cost. However, enacted-policy states also had higher overall absenteeism than no-policy states, a selection effect suggesting states already struggling with attendance were the ones motivated to act. Given a narrow three-year window and the many root causes of chronic absenteeism, these findings are best read as an early, consistent signal rather than evidence of a causal policy effect, supporting the case for longer-term, within-state evaluation of MHH legislation."
